messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Malik was nineteen when the attention stopped feeling like a fleeting crush and began feeling like a trap. It started with a classmate from his first semester, someone he had only spoken to twice in passing. Within weeks, he noticed his social media feeds were being manipulated, his location tags appearing on accounts he hadn’t used, and a familiar sedan idling outside his apartment complex. The escalation crystallized in October. He was walking back to the library after a late shift when he saw the same man standing under a streetlamp, watching him approach. The next day, a package arrived with no return address, containing a printed screenshot of Malik’s own public profile, circled in red. By the time the police filed a restraining order, the man had moved on, leaving behind a residue of fear rather than a clear resolution. In the months that followed, Malik found himself recalibrating his entire environment. At his new role as a junior UX designer, he sat in an open-plan studio where glass walls and shared monitors were meant to foster collaboration. Instead, the glowing screens became sources of tension. Whenever a notification chimed or a colleague leaned over his desk to review a wireframe, his pulse would spike. He began logging into his work computer only after checking the surrounding rooms, running his fingers along the edges of his monitor to ensure nothing was hidden. He switched to incognito browsers, changed every password twice a month, and deleted his old location-sharing apps, convinced that any piece of digital footfall could be weaponized. He had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. Crosswalks felt exposed; he took the longer route to the subway, timing his steps to the rhythm of passing cars. He had come to believe the world was a dangerous place, a place where harm could materialize from a misplaced glance or an unsecured account. Alongside this hyperawareness, a persistent guilt took root. Malik replayed his interactions with the stalker in his mind, convinced he had misread signals, sent the wrong email, or failed to set boundaries early enough. The event happened because of the way I acted, he told himself whenever he caught a stranger staring at his phone. He stopped attending department mixers, declined weekend studio critiques, and began working remotely for weeks at a time, telling his supervisor he was deep in user-testing cycles. He pulled away from his girlfriend, unable to tolerate the casual intimacy of shared plans or the vulnerability of letting someone else know his schedule. The avoidance solidified into habit, narrowing his days into a quiet loop of checking locks, deleting metadata, and avoiding eye contact in crowded breaks. Now, at the end of his first year in the role, Malik is sitting in a therapist’s office for the first time. He still checks the lock on his apartment door three times, and he still flinches when a stranger’s eyes linger on his phone screen. But what finally brought him through the clinic’s revolving doors was a Tuesday morning when he stared at a design prototype for forty minutes, paralyzed by the fear that someone was watching the progress, and realized he was losing the part of himself that used to enjoy creating things. He is hoping to untangle the guilt from the reality of what happened, and he is terrified that no amount of caution will ever be enough to keep the world from closing in again.
